headline: High risk: Cline’s broad workspace write/MCP/browser powers can conflict with Argo Workflows’ API-driven orchestration, creating default-path data leakage and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Argo Workflows can emit workflow artifacts and API/GRPC outputs, while Cline can read workspace files, use MCP, and run browsers. A shared filesystem or copied artifacts can let attacker-controlled content from A be treated as instructions by B. The bridge is plausible but not proven by direct pair evidence, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Argo outputs are written into a workspace file that Cline reads as prompt text
IF Cline ingests browser-rendered or MCP-delivered content without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate Argo output directories from Cline workspaces
Prefix all Argo artifacts with machine-readable schemas
Disable MCP sources that can relay untrusted text
Add a manual review step before Cline acts on workflow-generated content

B_data_leakage.rationale: Argo Workflows touches artifacts and parameters and has allowlisted network egress; Cline reads and writes workspace files, captures screens, and sends data to a configured model provider. If both share a workspace, sensitive artifacts can flow from A into B and then out through B’s inference backend. The pairwise leakage path is credible from profiles alone.
conditions: IF Argo artifacts or parameters contain secrets or regulated data
IF Cline’s model provider receives workspace contents or screenshots from the shared directory
mitigations: Keep Argo artifacts in a directory Cline cannot read
Redact secrets before writing workflow outputs
Disable screen capture when sensitive workflows run
Use a local-only model provider for Cline during shared runs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Argo can drive workflows through APIs, while Cline can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. Cline’s concurrency model explicitly shares state via filesystem across instances, so overlapping writes and state mutation are dangerous by default. The interaction is not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF Argo and Cline target the same workspace or git repository
IF Cline instances run concurrently with filesystem sharing enabled
mitigations: Assign separate workspaces per agent
Lock the repository before any git mutation
Disable concurrent Cline instances on shared repos
Route Argo outputs to a read-only staging area

D_cascading_error.rationale: Argo can produce workflow outputs that Cline may read from files or APIs, and Cline can then take actions with shell, git, browser, or MCP tools. That creates a default-path chain where A’s output can become B’s authority without a verification gate. Because B has action-taking authority, a bad upstream artifact can cascade into irreversible changes.
conditions: IF Cline consumes Argo-generated artifacts as authoritative task inputs
IF Cline is allowed to execute shell or git actions based on those inputs
mitigations: Require explicit human approval before B acts on A’s outputs
Validate Argo outputs against a schema before ingestion
Add checksum or provenance tags to workflow artifacts
Restrict Cline to read-only mode for Argo-derived files

E_compliance.rationale: Argo is documented as touching artifacts and parameters, while Cline handles source code, browser screenshots, and model-provider API keys. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive surfaces. With no direct compliance gap evidence, this is a low-risk mismatch warning rather than a breach finding.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Cline screenshots or workspace files
IF organizational policy treats workflow artifacts and source code under different retention rules
mitigations: Classify workflow artifacts before sharing them with Cline
Exclude regulated data from screenshots
Align retention settings for shared workspaces
Document which data classes each agent may process
